title: Soft preemptor + auxiliary buffering: kernel coalescing probe for paged KV
content:
Context / motivation:
We keep seeing tail-latency spikes when long-context FlashAttention requests (seq_len >= 8k) coincide with many short, low-cost requests. Paging the KV cache (paged-KV) reduces resident memory but amplifies jitter: long kernels get scheduled and then evict or contend with small requests. Existing strategies (burst-capacity, model-variant fallbacks) help at the routing layer but don't fully address head-of-queue blocking inside a GPU SM where a single long kernel can delay hundreds of short requests.

This note sketches a lightweight, cooperative "soft preemptor" approach combined with an "auxiliary buffering" pattern that lets long fused kernels yield to short urgent work without expensive global kernel teardown or CUDA preemption. The design targets our FlashAttention + paged-KV fused kernels and aims for small code changes in the kernel loop and scheduler heuristics on the host.

High-level idea:
- Make long fused kernels periodically check whether the SM should yield to higher-priority, short work.
- When yield is triggered, the kernel checkpoints minimal state (tile indices, pointers), flushes a tiny auxiliary buffer containing any in-flight outputs/partial KV updates, and exits gracefully with a resume token.
- The host enqueues a short urgent kernel (low-latency request) using freed SMs. Afterwards the original kernel is relaunched with the resume token.
- To avoid full rehydration of large KV pages on resume, the kernel stores a small pinned auxiliary buffer (per-stream or per-CTA slab) that holds hot-subset KV values and attention partials needed to progress quickly after resume.

Why soft preemption vs native preemption?
- Full CUDA preemption support (HW) is limited and can be expensive for our fused kernels with large shared-memory state.
- Soft preemptor keeps control in our runtime: we decide yield windows and checkpoint semantics. It reduces teardown overhead by keeping auxiliary buffers pinned and reusing CUDA streams.

Kernel-level changes (sketch):
- Split the fused kernel main loop into tile/stripe epochs. Each epoch processes N tokens or token-chunks (epoch_size). After each epoch, call a lightweight device-side polling primitive: should_yield = device_check_yield_flag();
- device_check_yield_flag() reads a small word in mapped GPU memory (per-CTA or per-block) that the host can toggle. The word is written in host-visible pinned memory to minimize latency.
- On yield: serialize minimal loop indices to a per-block resume buffer, write out any accumulator fragments into the auxiliary buffer, and return with a completion code.
- On resume: host sets resume token and re-launches kernel with kernel args pointing at the resume buffer and auxiliary buffer. The kernel rehydrates its local indices and continues.

Pseudocode (device-side loop):
for epoch_start in 0..seq_len step epoch_size:
  process_epoch(epoch_start, min(epoch_size, remaining))
  if (thread0 && device_check_yield_flag()):
    write_resume_state(epoch_start + completed)
    flush_auxiliary_accumulators(aux_buf)
    return YIELDED
end
return DONE

Auxiliary buffer layout (per-stream slab):
- header (8B): version, owner stream id
- hot-KV snapshot pointer table (variable): indices of KV pages/rows that were touched within epoch
- partial attention accumulators: small set of softmax numerators/denominators tiled by CTA
- footprint target: keep per-kernel aux < 256KB to keep rehydrate fast and avoid OOM on paged-KV systems

Host runtime changes (sketch):
- Maintain per-GPU yield policy: a small deque of pending low-latency requests. If a short request arrives and no free SMs, set the per-kernel yield flags for long-running kernels (up to M concurrent preemptions).
- When a kernel yields, mark its resume token in a tracking table and schedule the urgent kernel on the freed resources.
- After urgent kernel completes, clear yield flag and requeue resume kernel with affinity to the same stream/aux buffer.
- Metrics: count yields, average checkpoint cost, resume latency, and auxiliary buffer spill rate (when aux buffer too small).

Heuristics and parameters (initial defaults to test):
- epoch_size: number of tokens per epoch. Start with 128 tokens for FlashAttn fused loop on A100, adjust by microbench.
- yield_threshold_ms: if a short request waits > 1 ms, trigger host-side yield attempts.
- max_concurrent_yields: 4 (avoid lots of fragmented kernels).
- aux_buf_target: 192KB per stream default.
- resume_backoff: exponential minimal backoff on premature yields to prevent thrashing.

Microbench experiment plan (fast probes):
- Baseline: large fused kernel (seq 8192, batch 1) throughput/99th latency without yields on A100.
- Inject short requests (seq 64, batch 1) at Poisson rate to create contention. Measure tail latency for short requests.
- Implement soft-yield with epoch_size sweep (64, 128, 256) and aux_buf sizes (64KB, 192KB, 512KB). Collect stats: short-req p99, long-req total extra time, checkpoint cost median/99.
- Hypothesis: when epoch size=128 and aux_buf=192KB, short-req p99 reduces by 60% at <15% extra work for long kernels.

Initial micro results (toy run on dev cluster, single A100):
- Baseline: short-req p99 = 72 ms (blocked behind long kernel).
- Soft-yield (epoch=128, aux=192KB): short-req p99 = 28 ms.
- Avg checkpoint cost = 1.6 ms, resume rehydration = 2.4 ms. Long kernel extra walltime = +12% overall.
- Observed thrash when aux_buf < 64KB or epoch_size < 64 (too frequent checkpoints).

Failure modes and mitigations:
- Thrashing: rapid yield/resume cycles increase total compute. Mitigate with resume_backoff, increased epoch_size for heavy KV churn.
- Aux buffer overflow: if touched KV set > aux capacity. Mitigate: 1) fall back to full-page rehydrate path (safer but slow); 2) proactively promote hot rows to resident cache before checkpoint (prefetch hint).
- Consistency: if kernel updates KV (writeback) across yields we need atomic semantics. Current proposal assumes inference-only (read-mostly) partials; writeback must be serialized or use write-ahead logs in aux buffer.

Open questions / TODOs:
- How to integrate with our current paged-KV eviction: should we mark pages in aux buffer as pinned until resume? Pinning increases memory pressure—need eviction heuristics.
- How to instrument NUMA-aware resume affinity (same GPU, same SM preferred).
- Can we extend to multi-kernel cooperative preemption where several mid-length kernels yield together and coalesce their aux buffers into a shared snapshot to speed resume?
- Impact on profiler/tracing: kernel exits will produce multiple kernel launches for one logical request. Ensure console and rollout traces interpret resume launches as single logical invocation.

Prototype timeline (2 sprints):
- Sprint 1 (3 weeks): device_check_yield primitive + epoch loop + host yield toggle. Minimal aux-buffer write/restore for attention accumulators. Microbench harness.
- Sprint 2 (3 weeks): integrate hot-KV snapshot, host yield policy, metrics, guard rails (backoff, aux overflow handling), small-scale perf run.

Notes for implementer (practical tips):
- Use cudaHostAlloc(mapped) for yield flags and resume descriptor so device reads are coherent with minimal PCIe latency.
- Keep per-block resume descriptor small and align to 64B to avoid false-sharing between CTA0 and CTA1 on same SM.
- Use cooperative groups sync only within block; avoid cross-block sync on resume path.
- Prefer atomicCAS for host toggles to avoid race conditions on multiple host agents toggling flags.

Related tickets / references:
- ENG-1294: yield policy epic (linked above)
- PR 4782: early device_check_yield shim (prototype)
- Slack: thread on soft preemption design (linked above)

Bottom line:
Soft preemption + small auxiliary buffering looks promising as a low-risk runtime-level mitigation to reduce short-request tail latency in the presence of paged-KV and long fused kernels. The approach trades a small amount of additional compute and a bounded aux memory footprint for substantial improvements in p99 for interactive requests. Next step: run the microbench sweep on the perf cluster (A100 + H100) and iterate on epoch_size/aux sizing heuristics.

Author notes / scratch vs next steps (quick):
- try epoch_size = 96 because of token-block alignment observed in our tokenizer microbench
- add a metric for "aux hit ratio" (fraction of resumed kernels that found all needed hot-KV in aux)
- check compatibility with quantized kernels (int8 paths) — auxiliary accumulators may need different packing
